sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Centralization**: Akbar shifted from a tribal-military structure to a **bureaucratic-civilian** model. 
• **Separation of Powers**: Distinct separation between **Revenue (Diwan)** and **Military/Executive (Mir Bakshi)** functions to prevent power concentration. 
• **Provincial Uniformity**: The empire was divided into **Subahs** (provinces) with a standardized administrative hierarchy to ensure uniform tax collection and law enforcement. 
• **Key Metric**: The **Mansabdari System** served as the backbone, integrating military rank with civil administrative responsibility.

items.definition: Initially the Prime Minister (e.g., Bairam Khan), but Akbar reduced this office's power after 1560 to prevent the rise of a 'de facto' ruler.
Head of the military department; responsible for intelligence, recruitment, and maintaining the descriptive rolls (Chehra) of soldiers.
Head of religious endowments and charities; acted as the chief advisor on religious matters.
Executive head of a Sarkar (district); responsible for law and order and assisting in revenue collection.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Dahsala System**: Raja Todar Mal's revenue reform based on 10-year average yields. 
• **Subah System**: Formalized in 1580, dividing the empire into 12 (later 15) Subahs.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Over-reliance on the personality of the Emperor; potential for corruption in the Mansabdari hierarchy. 
• **Solutions**: Regular transfers of officials and the use of the 'Waqia-navis' (news writers) to report directly to the center.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'V-D-B-S' (Vakil, Diwan, Bakshi, Sadr). 
• **Decoded Meaning**: V (Vakil-PM), D (Diwan-Finance), B (Bakshi-Military), S (Sadr-Religious).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses 'Mir Bakshi' (Military) with 'Mir Saman' (Royal Household/Karkhanas). Remember: Bakshi = Battle/Military.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Institutionalized Autocracy' to describe Akbar's administration, highlighting how he balanced personal power with a structured bureaucracy.

keyTakeaways: Akbar's administration was a blend of Persian administrative theory and Indian socio-political realities.
The separation of the Diwan (Revenue) and Subahdar (Executive) was a deliberate mechanism to prevent provincial rebellion.
The Mansabdari system was the singular institution that unified the military and civil services under one hierarchy.
